Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application for uploading, browsing, viewing, and deleting images. This source-based assessment describes the implemented architecture and optional Docker Compose topology; it does not verify a running deployment.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Browser - HTML and JavaScript upload UI"] end subgraph Application["Application Layer - Spring Boot 2.7.18 on Java 8"] Security["Spring Security - HTTP Basic"] MVC["Spring MVC - gallery, upload, detail and image endpoints"] Views["Thymeleaf templates"] Business["Photo business services - validation and navigation"] Image["Java ImageIO - image dimensions"] end subgraph Data["Data Access Layer"] Persistence["Spring Data JPA and Hibernate"] Driver["Oracle JDBC"] end subgraph Storage["Database Storage"] Oracle[("Oracle Database - photo metadata and BLOBs")] Volume[("Docker named volume - Oracle data")] end subgraph External["External Services"] CDN["jsDelivr - Bootstrap 5.3.0 assets"] end Browser -->|"HTTP on port 8080"| Security Security -->|"public reads and authenticated upload or delete"| MVC MVC -->|"view models"| Views Views -->|"rendered HTML"| Browser Browser -->|"HTTPS asset requests"| CDN MVC -->|"photo operations"| Business Business -->|"inspect uploaded image headers"| Image Business -->|"transactional reads and writes"| Persistence Persistence -->|"JPA and native SQL"| Driver Driver -->|"JDBC on port 1521 in Compose"| Oracle Oracle -->|"Compose persistence"| Volume MVC -->|"image bytes or upload JSON"| Browser

Data Storage & External Services

The photos table stores UUID identifiers, filenames, size, MIME type, upload timestamp, dimensions, and image bytes in a BLOB. Uploads persist bytes in Oracle, and image requests read those bytes through the application; stored file paths are compatibility metadata, not the active upload storage mechanism. Compose defines separate application and Oracle containers on a bridge network, with a named Oracle data volume and mounted initialization scripts. Both application profiles configure Hibernate schema creation (ddl-auto=create), so a database volume alone does not guarantee preservation of application tables on restart. Browser pages load Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr. No cache, message broker, object-storage integration, or backend remote API client was identified in the inspected application source.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor-injected controllers, a PhotoService interface and implementation, and a Spring Data repository; service-level transactions cover persistence operations.
  • Images and metadata share the relational database. Native repository queries use Oracle-specific constructs, including ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR.
  • Gallery and image reads are public; upload and delete POST routes require authentication. Security uses an in-memory administrator with BCrypt, stateless HTTP Basic, and disabled CSRF; configuration values and credentials are intentionally omitted.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicitly mapped HTTP endpoints provide gallery HTML, photo bytes, multipart upload, and deletion. Browser requests and server-side operations are synchronous request/response interactions; no backend messaging or inter-service HTTP API was found.

The build has one module. Application dependencies include Spring Boot 2.7.18 Web/MVC, Thymeleaf, Data JPA, Security, Validation, JSON/Jackson, and the Oracle JDBC driver. No additional deployable application modules, gateway, discovery service, or observability service were identified.

API Endpoints Inventory

All endpoints belong to photoalbum-java-app. No URL, header, or query-based API versioning is implemented.

Service / ControllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
App / HomeControllerGET/No bound parameters200 HTML index view, populated from List; retrieval exceptions produce an empty gallery rather than an error response.
App / HomeControllerPOST/uploadMultipart form with repeated files parts bound to List; HTTP Basic authentication200 JSON Map containing upload outcomes, including partial or total per-file rejection; 400 JSON for the explicit empty-list guard; missing required parts normally produce framework 400; unauthenticated requests receive 401.
App / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}String path parameter id200 HTML detail view using Photo and neighboring-photo identifiers; redirect to / (normally 302) for missing photos or caught exceptions.
App / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deleteString path parameter id; HTTP Basic authentication; no request DTORedirect to / (normally 302) with success/error flash attributes, including not-found and caught failure outcomes; unauthenticated requests receive 401.
App / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path parameter id; browser also sends an ignored _t cache-busting query parameter200 Resource backed by ByteArrayResource, with the stored MIME type; 404 for missing photo or absent bytes; 500 for caught exceptions.

Contract details

  • Upload JSON uses success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads; the explicit empty-list error uses success and error instead. Clients must inspect per-file outcomes even on HTTP 200. There is no typed upload-response DTO or uniform error envelope.
  • Application-level file rejection normally appears inside HTTP 200, not HTTP 400. Multipart parsing/size failures occur before controller handling; no custom multipart exception contract was found.
  • A successful upload is followed by a separate metadata lookup before it is included in the response. Lookup failures are not caught by HomeController.uploadPhotos; the response is not an atomic batch-success guarantee.
  • Photo responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size. No explicit content-disposition, range, ETag, or conditional-download handling is implemented by the controller.
  • Templates also reference framework-served static CSS/JavaScript. The legacy /uploads/ path returned in metadata is not the current database-backed photo-serving contract; clients use /photo/{id}.
  • Framework-provided static-resource and error handling are not additional explicitly mapped business endpoints.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: Browser GETs and multipart POSTs invoke MVC controllers, which call PhotoService directly. PhotoServiceImpl invokes PhotoRepository through JPA/JDBC. No REST client, Feign, gRPC, or calls to independently deployed business APIs were found.
  • Browser interaction: JavaScript uses fetch('/upload') and then updates the gallery from JSON; image bytes are fetched separately. JavaScript async/await does not represent asynchronous backend messaging. Templates load Bootstrap CSS/JavaScript from an external HTTPS CDN; this is browser asset delivery, not server-to-server business communication.
  • Asynchronous: No broker, pub/sub, event bus, background API job, WebSocket, or server-sent event contract identified.
  • Gateway/discovery/load balancing: None identified. Browser paths are same-origin. Compose provides a database service hostname; no application service registration or client-side load balancer is implemented. No cross-service aggregation or downstream fallback exists.
  • Resilience: No application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, explicit outbound request timeout, or application-configured JDBC timeout was identified. Browser upload has no explicit timeout/AbortController and offers a manual retry message, not automatic retry. Compose restarts the application on failure; this is process recovery, not request retry.
  • Failure behavior: Gallery retrieval falls back to an empty list; detail and delete handlers redirect on caught failures. Upload processing is sequential per file, returning internal failures as per-file results where caught. Transaction completion or the subsequent metadata lookup can still fail outside the returned UploadResult; no controller-wide handler guarantees JSON for such failures. Binary retrieval returns 404 or 500 as described above.
  • Availability: Compose starts the application after the database becomes healthy. Required administrative credentials must also be supplied for the security bean to initialize. Deployment/configuration details belong in /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java/PhotoAlbum-Java/.github/modernize/assessment/copilot/engines/facts/configuration-inventory.md.
  • Authentication/authorization: Stateless HTTP Basic protects POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete. Other requests are permitted without authentication. An in-memory administrator principal is configured, but endpoint rules require only authentication, not an ADMIN role check or per-photo ownership check. No JWT/OAuth2 or method-level authorization was found. CSRF is disabled; no login-page endpoint is configured.
  • Transport: The application/container expose HTTP 8080; no application TLS configuration or HTTPS enforcement was identified. CDN asset requests use HTTPS, but that does not secure the application's HTTP Basic credentials. External TLS termination cannot be confirmed from these application contracts.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared photo collection, inspect individual images, and navigate by upload chronology. Authenticated users can add photos in batches and permanently remove photos.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo CollectionAn uploaded image and its descriptive information, managed as one business record. This is the sole persistent domain entity found.Displayed in the shared gallery; related to older and newer photos through upload chronology, not explicit entity associations.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload ProcessingA transient outcome for one attempted upload, not a persistent entity or aggregate.Identifies the saved Photo on success, or associates the attempted filename with an error on failure.

No separate Album, photo owner, tagging, or user-profile domain entities were found. The gallery is a collection view, not a stored album aggregate.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

The application is a single deployable service. The following are internal responsibilities, not independently deployed microservices.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto collection, upload acceptance, chronological navigation, removalPhoto; transient UploadResultPhotoRepository and the database containing photo content and metadata
HomeControllerGallery presentation and batch-upload orchestrationNone; composes Photo summaries and upload outcomesInternal PhotoService; browser upload interface
DetailControllerIndividual-photo viewing and deletion feedbackNone; composes current Photo and neighboring photo identifiersInternal PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerDelivery of stored image contentNone; reads Photo contentInternal PhotoService

PhotoService is the business entry to the repository; the database is the source of truth for both content and metadata. There is no separately owned media-storage service or cross-context identifier exchange.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and publish accepted photos

  1. A visitor selects or drops files in the gallery. The browser applies Client upload screening, then sends accepted candidates to POST /upload.
  2. The security boundary requires authentication under Mutation authorization. The controller applies Nonempty batch.
  3. The controller processes files sequentially through PhotoService. Each file follows Server upload acceptance and Image dimension handling.
  4. For an accepted file, the service generates a compatibility filename and path, reads image content, optionally extracts dimensions, constructs a Photo, and saves its content and metadata together. The compatibility path is not a file-system write or the image-delivery source.
  5. The service returns an UploadResult. For each successful result, the controller reads the Photo back and adds a summary to the batch response. Failed results become filename-associated errors.
  6. Batch outcome aggregation permits partial success; accepted files are not intentionally undone because another file is rejected. The browser prepends returned photos to the gallery and shows per-file errors. Image content is fetched separately from GET /photo/{id}.

An upload can be stored without a returned summary if its follow-up lookup returns empty. A thrown follow-up lookup error is not caught by the upload controller, so response completion is not guaranteed even after earlier files have been saved.

Workflow 2: Browse the gallery and navigate photo details

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController loads all photos through PhotoService and renders the gallery under Gallery ordering.
  2. The browser requests image content separately for each displayed Photo identifier.
  3. Selecting a photo opens GET /detail/{id}. DetailController loads the selected Photo, obtains older and newer neighbors under Chronological navigation, and renders metadata and available navigation links.
  4. The detail image is delivered through GET /photo/{id} using the same stored Photo record.
  5. Under Read degradation, gallery retrieval failure produces an empty gallery; a missing detail record or detail-loading exception redirects to the gallery. Missing image content produces a not-found response rather than a replacement image.

Workflow 3: Permanently remove a photo

  1. The detail page asks for browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete; cancellation prevents that browser submission.
  2. Mutation authorization is checked before the controller runs.
  3. PhotoService looks up the Photo. A missing record returns a negative outcome; an existing record is deleted, including its stored image content.
  4. DetailController sets success, not-found, or failure feedback and redirects to the gallery.

There is no soft-delete, trash, restore, approval, or separate media-cleanup workflow in the inspected implementation. Browser confirmation is not a server-side business precondition.

No scheduled jobs, message-driven business handlers, batch commands, or startup routines that initialize business records were found in the application sources. Repository methods for month filtering, pagination, and statistics have no traced controller/service workflow and are not treated as exposed business processes.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend-to-backend business service calls, event exchanges, gateway aggregations, or circuit breakers in the inspected sources.

  • Batch composition: HomeController combines per-file UploadResult outcomes with follow-up Photo reads into successful summaries and failed-upload messages. Summaries are associated by the saved Photo identifier.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines a current Photo with older and newer Photo identifiers from repository queries. This is in-process composition within one collection context.
  • Content delivery: Gallery and detail pages refer to images by Photo identifier. Separate browser requests retrieve bytes from the same source-of-truth record; compatibility upload paths are not used for this delivery.
  • Availability outcomes: Database read failures can appear as an empty gallery or a redirect rather than explicit unavailability. Image-serving exceptions return a server error; upload read/save failures generally become per-file errors. There is no alternative storage provider, queue, retry, or compensating operation.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and acceptance

  • Client upload screening: The browser permits JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP MIME types and files up to 10 MiB. It does not reject zero-byte files or enforce a file-count limit.
  • Nonempty batch: A null or empty file list is rejected with a bad-request response. Files missing at request binding may be rejected before controller execution.
  • Server upload acceptance: A file's declared content type, lowercased, must match the configured allowed MIME types. Its size must be positive and no greater than the configured byte limit. Checked-in settings allow the same four image types and 10 MiB per file. A missing content type falls into the generic upload-error path.
  • Request envelope: Checked-in multipart settings limit each file to 10 MB and the entire request to 50 MB; these limits can reject a request before per-file processing. A configured maximum of ten files is not consumed by the inspected upload controller, service, or browser script, so it is not an implemented file-count rule.
  • Image dimension handling: Where an image reader recognizes the content, width multiplied by height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. Dimensions are read from the header. An I/O failure rejects the file; no reader or a non-I/O extraction exception permits continuation without dimensions. Declared MIME acceptance therefore does not guarantee recognized or fully decoded image content.
  • Photo metadata constraints: Entity declarations require nonblank original and generated filenames, each at most 255 characters; a nonblank MIME type at most 50 characters; positive, nonnull file size; nonnull upload time; and a compatibility path at most 500 characters. Image dimensions are optional. These persistence constraints are distinct from explicit upload checks; image content is nullable in the entity and the delivery workflow handles absent content.

Decisions and lifecycle

  • Batch outcome aggregation: Each service upload is a separate transaction, not one batch-wide transaction. The controller marks overall success only when at least one saved Photo summary is included. Individual rejected uploads normally still produce an HTTP-success batch response containing failure details.
  • Gallery ordering: All photos are retrieved newest first. Browser-inserted upload results are prepended; a full reload restores database timestamp ordering.
  • Chronological navigation: Previous means the nearest strictly older upload; next means the nearest strictly newer upload. The service takes the first query result. Photos with equal upload timestamps are not neighbors through these strict comparisons, and no identifier tie-breaker is specified. Navigation ends when the relevant result list is empty.
  • Identity and uniqueness: New Photos receive generated identifiers and upload timestamps; generated storage names retain the original extension. No content deduplication or original-filename uniqueness rule is implemented.
  • Lifecycle: A candidate is rejected or becomes a persisted Photo; a persisted Photo can be viewed and permanently deleted. These are workflow outcomes, not a stored status state machine. There are no approval or archival states and no bidirectional entity relationships to maintain.
  • Presentation calculations: File sizes are displayed in human-readable units and dimensions only when available; no pricing, quotas per user, or other calculated business totals are implemented.

Cross-cutting behavior

  • Mutation authorization: Upload and delete require an authenticated caller via HTTP Basic. The configured account is assigned an administrator role, but endpoint checks require authentication rather than explicitly testing that role. Read requests are public. No per-photo ownership restrictions exist in the inspected domain.
  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional; lookup/list/navigation methods are read-only transactions. Photo content and metadata are saved or deleted through the same record. Some persistence errors can surface during transaction completion after the method's local save handling, so a caught save error is not a guarantee of a complete batch response.
  • Read degradation: Gallery errors are logged and rendered as an empty collection, which can resemble a genuinely empty album. Detail errors or missing records redirect to the gallery. Image requests with blank identifiers, missing records, or absent bytes return not found; other serving failures return a server error. Image responses discourage caching, favoring current content over reuse.
  • Deletion errors: Missing records yield not-found feedback; exceptions yield generic retry feedback. No explicit retry or compensation is implemented.
  • Audit and logging: Upload acceptance/rejection, deletion, retrieval failures, and image serving are logged. Image-serving diagnostics also log a small content prefix. No persistent business audit entity, uploader attribution, or durable change history was found.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is outside open-source support; its managed Spring Framework 5.3.31, Spring Security 5.7.11, Hibernate 5.6.15.Final, and Thymeleaf 3.0.15.RELEASE represent an aging stack. These are BOM-managed versions, not additional direct dependencies. Moving to Spring Boot 3 or later requires at least Java 17 rather than the declared Java 8 target and involves Java EE javax to Jakarta namespace migration. Commons IO 2.11.0 is an older explicit pin outside Boot version management. Oracle JDBC 21.5.0.0 and test H2 2.1.214 should be reviewed for current support and compatibility before upgrades. No vulnerability scan or runtime compatibility test was performed; no specific CVE finding is asserted.

Notable Observations

  • Only one recognized build manifest was found, with no declared Maven modules or dependency lockfiles. Transitive resolution was not executed; BOM membership alone does not establish that a library is on the application classpath.
  • Boot supplies version management for every direct dependency except Commons IO. The Oracle driver's version comes through an imported Oracle BOM, not a version explicitly written in the application POM.
  • The JSON starter supplies JSON support, not an image-processing library despite its adjacent POM comment. Its declaration overlaps the standard Web starter's JSON support; no independent image-processing dependency is declared.
  • DevTools is optional but retains default compile scope. The Spring Boot Maven plugin is also declared without a version; it is build tooling and is excluded from dependency counts and the diagram.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA and Hibernate to Oracle, with image bytes and metadata stored together. An H2 in-memory database is configured for the test profile.

Database Configuration

Service/ModuleDB TypeProfileDriverConnectionMigration Tool
Photo AlbumOracle; local configuration identifies Oracle Database Free 23ai, but the image tag is floatingDefaultcom.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc8; oracle.jdbc.OracleDriverEnvironment-overridable JDBC Thin connection to an Oracle pluggable database; authentication supplied externally; no explicit pool tuning foundNo Flyway or Liquibase; Hibernate recreates the mapped schema at startup
Photo AlbumOracledockerSame Oracle runtime driverEnvironment-overridable JDBC Thin connection; external credentials; no explicit pool tuning foundHibernate recreates the mapped schema at startup
Photo Album testsH2 in-memorytestcom.h2database:h2 (test scope); org.h2.DriverProcess-local, in-memory JDBC database; H2 dialectHibernate creates the schema and drops it when the persistence factory closes
  • Schema authority: entity mappings, not versioned SQL migrations. Runtime profiles request schema recreation, so existing photo data can be lost across application restarts even if database storage survives.
  • Initialization: Oracle initialization SQL grants schema privileges and checks account/database availability; it does not define photos or seed photo records. No photo seed SQL or programmatic data initializer was found in the inspected source.
  • Pooling: the JPA starter normally supplies HikariCP through its JDBC dependencies; no application-defined datasource, pool sizes, or timeout overrides were found. This is dependency-based inference, not a runtime observation.
  • Portability: repository queries use Oracle-specific SQL, and the entity includes Oracle-specific numeric and timestamp DDL. The H2 profile alone does not establish that these mappings or queries are compatible with H2.
  • Full configuration-property inventory belongs in configuration-inventory.md; connection strings, credential values, and raw property assignments are intentionally omitted here.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application service owns one logical application schema containing photos. Image bytes and descriptive metadata share the same database and transactional boundary; no separate object store or active filesystem image store is used by the inspected persistence implementation.

There is no separate service-owned database, shared-database integration with another application, direct cross-service database access, or remote data-aggregation client in the inspected data layer. The H2 test profile substitutes an ephemeral database rather than adding a second production data owner. Reads and writes use the same entity and repository: read-only transaction annotations are optimizations, not CQRS separation.

There is no user/tenant identifier or ownership relationship on Photo. Authentication for photo mutations is application-wide rather than row-level or per-owner; gallery/photo reads are public in the inspected security configuration. The configured Oracle account has schema-object creation privileges for Hibernate, not an application-enforced per-record boundary.
